1.name: Clean Slate
1.big: A fresh start. Twelve core screens redrawn bright and simple in the three Pokémon logo colours (red, yellow, blue), replacing the dark navy look.
1.q1: Not yet. It is tidy but flat: square cards on dotted paper, small sprites, nothing moves. Next pass needs energy and scale.
1.q2: Against the game today: light instead of dark, far bigger words, one selection colour, and every button says what it does.
1.q3: Yes. The battle screen sends Bag and Pokémon to the general pages, which hides the fight. They need their own battle pages.
1.q4: The Pause Menu is a plain list and Settings is one long tab row. Both work, neither is special yet.
1.q5: Partly. The logo colours and Poké Ball markers say Pokémon, but the shapes could be any app.

2.name: Slant & Scale
2.big: Everything leans forward. A red slash carries every title, buttons and plates are slanted, sprites are about twice as big, and the battle gets its own Bag and Switch pages.
2.q1: Better: the slash and the huge Charizard on the title grab the eye. But it is still two flat colours with no life from the Pokémon themselves.
2.q2: Pass 1 was square cards on paper. Now panels lean, the lead Pokémon gets a big card, the map is a real road with stop numbers, and Fight is the biggest button in battle.
2.q3: Done here: Bag and Switch are battle pages now, so the fight stays on screen behind them. Move details still crowd the move row and should get more room.
2.q4: The Pause Menu moved onto the red slash with the trainer standing beside it. Settings swapped the tab row for a category list on the left, which leaves room for more categories.
2.q5: More than before. Slanted bars and a road map read as modern Pokémon. What is missing is type colour, the thing every Pokémon screen is built on.

3.name: Type Colour
3.big: Colour now means something. Moves, party cards, HP plates and the Summary are painted in the Pokémon's own type with type medals, and every move shows how well it will hit.
3.q1: Yes: move cards are big blocks of type colour with a ghosted medal, and the Summary band is a fire-to-sky gradient. It still sits perfectly still, which is the next thing to fix.
3.q2: Pass 2 used red, yellow and white for everything. Now a glance tells you type, matchup (▲ Super effective, ▼ Weak hit) and event risk (orange risky, green certain, blue costs money).
3.q3: Two added. Move Info takes the long move text and the damage estimate off the move row. The Type Chart gets its own page, opened with T from Party or Summary.
3.q4: No change to their layout this pass. Settings needs a colour-blind option now that colour carries meaning (planned with the accessibility pass); medals and arrows already repeat what the colour says.
3.q5: Much more. Type colours and type medals are the most Pokémon thing on any screen.

4.name: In Motion
4.big: Nothing sits still any more. The cursor is a hopping Poké Ball, the title band runs, sprites breathe over ground shadows, cards deal in one by one, pages slide and morph, and entering a battle is a Poké Ball that snaps shut and splits open.
4.q1: Yes in play: press Play tour or click around. The ball iris and the hit burst are the showpieces. On a still picture it reads through the ball cursor, ground shadows and the timeline strips.
4.q2: Pass 3 was a set of posters. Now every page has an entrance, every choice has a hopping ball and a breathing outline, HP drains with a ghost bar, and the map road marches toward the next stops.
4.q3: Two battle moments got their own pages so the animation can be designed step by step: Battle Start and Move Hit, each with a timeline. The Motion Sheet lists every animation and how long it takes.
4.q4: Menus slide in from the slash with the cards dealing in. Settings needs an Animations page where each effect can be turned down, and a Reduced motion switch that these mockups already obey.
4.q5: Yes. The ball opening on a wild Pokémon and the flash-shake-number of a hit are straight from the series.

5.name: Menu & Settings Hub
5.big: The Pause Menu is now a Poké Ball wheel with a live glance panel, Settings became a home page plus one page per category with real switches, sliders and a preview, and every area of the game has its own colour and badge in the title band.
5.q1: The wheel is the most eye-catching menu so far: eight badges orbit a Poké Ball with the trainer inside. Settings pages are calm on purpose, but they finally look like part of the game.
5.q2: Pass 4 still had a plain list for the menu and one cramped Settings list. Now the menu shows your party before you open anything, each setting has a proper control, and the title band changes colour by area with a trail showing where you are (Menu › Settings › Display).
5.q3: Five added. Settings alone went from one page to a home page and four category pages (the other categories follow the same pattern), plus Save Slots.
5.q4: This pass is the answer: Esc opens the wheel from anywhere, Settings is one stop on it, and Q and E flip between Settings categories without going back.
5.q5: Yes. The menu is literally a Poké Ball, and the Save Slots read like a trainer's journal.

6.name: Battle Stage
6.big: The battle is filmed like a movie. Dark bars at the top and bottom hold all the battle text, the camera sits right behind your Pokémon, and every menu now floats over the world instead of a blank page.
6.q1: Your Pokémon is drawn five times bigger from behind, the commands are round buttons that pop out of the bottom bar, and the lead of your party stands under a spotlight.
6.q2: Pass 5 still had small boxes floating over the arena. Now nothing floats: names, HP and text sit in two film bars, so the arena is clear and the Pokémon are huge.
6.q3: Yes, three. Throwing the ball, the trainer's VS intro and the ace reveal each get their own page, so the main battle screen never has to squeeze them in.
6.q4: The pause menu dims the world and puts a spotlight on the wheel. Settings and the other pages keep their layout but now show the world faintly behind them.
6.q5: Yes. The behind-the-back camera, the VS split and the Poké Ball throw are the classic Pokémon battle moments, just bigger.

7.name: Power Surge
7.big: Mega Evolution, Terastallizing, Dynamax and Z-Moves stop hiding inside the move list. They get a Power button, a picker page, a full-screen scene each, and a rainbow energy line that marks anything charged.
7.q1: Each power-up fills the whole screen with the game's own effect art: the Mega spiral, Tera crystals, the red Dynamax storm and the Z-Move title. The title screen now stars Mega Charizard X.
7.q2: Pass 6 had no place for power-ups at all. Now the battle bar has a glowing Power button, the Fight page shows what is armed, and the bars carry Mega, Tera, Max and Z tags.
7.q3: Yes, seven. One picker, four scenes, one page for the powered-up battle and a new Animations settings page.
7.q4: The pause menu and the Party page show which powers are ready, used or locked. Settings gets an Animations page where the scenes can be set to Full, Short or Off.
7.q5: Yes. These are the four big Pokémon battle gimmicks, shown the way the main games show them, with the game's own sprites and effects.

8.name: Victory Lap
8.big: Winning now feels like winning. The dark battle bar grows to fill the screen and walks you through seven clear steps: the win, team EXP, level up, a new move, evolution, a catch and a reward pick.
8.q1: A giant Victory banner with rays and an MVP badge, EXP bars that fill on six cards at once, a gold level stamp, and reward cards that deal in like a hand of cards.
8.q2: Before this pass a battle simply ended. Now EXP runs along the edge of the battle bar the whole time, the prize is shown during the fight, and every reward has its own screen.
8.q3: Yes, seven new pages. One job per page, so the level-up numbers, the move swap and the reward choice never fight for space.
8.q4: The pause menu shows the run score, stars and win streak. Header pills gain coin, badge and ball icons. The Animations settings from pass 7 also control these scenes.
8.q5: Yes. EXP bars, level-up stat lists, 'wants to learn a move', evolution with B to stop, and 'Gotcha!' are the heart of every Pokémon game.

9.name: Story Time
9.big: An event now plays like a small scene in four beats: talk, choose, result, reward. The place fills the screen, whoever speaks gets a face, and the text box waits for you every time.
9.q1: Full-screen place art with the hour and weather, a tall speaker with a portrait in the text box, and choices as three big cards that deal in with a coloured risk label.
9.q2: Pass 8 still showed the speech and all the choices crammed on one screen. Now the text stays alone until you press Enter, the choices get a clean page, and rewards only appear after the text is gone, as you asked.
9.q3: Yes, five. Choice, result and reward pages, an Event Stage page for battles that happen inside an event, and a Run Journal that lists every stop of this run.
9.q4: The pause menu and the title show the next stop and open the Journal with J. The map's Story button opens it too. Speaker portraits also appear in the shop and in the battle bar.
9.q5: Yes. A character talks, you answer, something happens. It reads like the story scenes of the main games, and the Journal works like a trainer's diary.

10.name: World Tour
10.big: The run becomes a trip around the world. Every region gets its own two colours and a passport stamp, the stage map is drawn on the region's real town map, and the region's colours ride on the battle bars.
10.q1: The title screen now sits on the Kanto town map with a tape of region colours behind the team. Entering a region gets a full-screen intro with a giant name and a stamp that thumps down.
10.q2: Before, a region was just a word in the header. Now it has colours, a stamp and a map you can recognise at a glance, and each Pokémon shows where it was met.
10.q3: Yes, four. World Tour shows all nine regions and what gets harder in each, Region Intro asks about regional forms, Badge Case shows the gyms and the League, and Gameplay settings holds stage length.
10.q4: The pause menu gets the region stamp and a stage progress line. Settings gets a Gameplay page with stage length, regional forms, Blessings, Ultra Beasts and Evil Mode.
10.q5: Yes. Town maps, gym badges in a case, the Elite Four and a new region with new rules are exactly how a Pokémon journey is measured.

11.name: Town Square
11.big: Places become places. The hub is a street built from the game's own buildings, your team walks beside you out of their balls, and the shop has real shelves and a counter.
11.q1: The title screen is now the town itself: a blue sky, the street, and Red leading the whole team along the road. In the hub, the building you are standing at glows and a big sign pops up over it.
11.q2: The hub used to be a row of seven tiles under a line-up. Now you walk a street and each door is a building. In battle the rest of the team waits on the sideline with little HP bars, and the party stage and pause menu show the place you are in.
11.q3: Yes, four. Check Out is its own page so the shelf stays clean, the Pokémon Center has its own healing page, and the Event Hall and Achievement Hall take the news and rewards off the hub.
11.q4: Settings is the last door on the street and still opens the Settings hub. The pause menu's ball is now a window onto where you are, with your partner walking next to you.
11.q5: More than any pass so far: Pokémon Center, Poké Mart, the route gate, a clerk behind the counter, the healing machine lighting up six balls one by one, and Pokémon following their trainer.

12.name: Collector's Cards
12.big: Every Pokémon is now a card you hold. The party is a hand of six shiny cards, the summary is one big card with a page for each tab, and the same card shows up in the Reserve, the pause menu and on the battle sideline.
12.q1: Cards have a type-coloured frame, a foil shine that sweeps across the picture and a gold level pill. They deal onto the table one after another. The stats page draws a six-point radar that grows out from the middle.
12.q2: The party was a big stage plus five rows. Now all six are equal cards side by side, so you can compare them at a glance. The summary used to cram seven tabs on one page; now there are three pages with room to breathe.
12.q3: Yes, six: Moves and Bond pages for the summary, a Pokédex and its entry page, the Reserve, and a Use On page so picking who gets a potion never covers the bag.
12.q4: The pause menu's party panel is now six small cards, and the wheel opens the Pokédex. Nothing new is needed in Settings; card shine follows the Animations setting from pass 7.
12.q5: Yes. Collecting cards is as Pokémon as it gets, and the Pokédex grid with grey unseen slots and Poké Ball marks is straight from the games.

13.name: Trainers
13.big: People get faces and colours. Each trainer has a colour that fills their banner, their Trainer Card and their side of the battle bars. Five new pages cover who you play as, your rivals, the next Gym Leader and the League.
13.q1: The title screen now has Red standing large in front of the town with a name plate. Trainer Select is a row of tall coloured banners, and the Trainer Card is a real card with a photo, a badge strip and a foil shine.
13.q2: Before, trainers were only a name on a bar. Now Blue's battle bar is blue and yours is red, so you can tell the sides apart before reading a word, and rivals have a board that shows the score between you.
13.q3: Yes, five. Trainer Select and the Trainer Card leave the hub and menu clean, the Rival Board holds all four rivals, the Gym Leader File shows what a boss brings before you commit, and the League is a staircase of five rooms.
13.q4: The pause menu swaps its row of pills for a one-line Trainer Card that opens the full card. No new settings are needed.
13.q5: Yes: a Trainer Card with eight badge slots, a rival who is always one step ahead, and a Gym Leader with a title and an ace are the heart of a Pokémon journey. The trainer is still not drawn on the battlefield itself.

14.name: Rotom Phone
14.big: One helper, one device. The pause menu is now a Rotom Phone with eight apps, Rotom gives one short tip wherever you might be stuck, and finding your way gets pages of its own.
14.q1: The phone is a big orange device with Rotom's blinking eyes and a lightning ear, and its apps pop in two by two. Rotom itself floats and tilts on every page it speaks on. Between stops the whole team walks along a scrolling road.
14.q2: The pause menu was a wheel that only held eight links. The phone holds the apps, the time, the next stop, a tip, your hand of cards and your powers in one tidy place. The old wheel stays as a quick pop-up on Tab.
14.q3: Yes, seven. Ask Rotom, Search, a Controls overlay for the page you are on, Notices, a Confirm box, a Travel screen and the Quick Wheel. None of them add anything to the pages you already use.
14.q4: The Menu is the phone. Settings is an app on it, Search can jump straight to one setting, and the Controls overlay points to Settings › Controls for changing keys.
14.q5: Yes, the Rotom Phone comes straight from the newer games. In this game the helper is always called Rotom.

15.name: The Journey
15.big: A run now has a clear beginning and a clear end. A route line with the eight gyms on it rides on every screen, and starting a run, picking a starter and a Blessing, losing and winning each get their own pages.
15.q1: The Hall of Fame puts each team member in its own spotlight with confetti. Blessings are dealt out as three tall cards with the Legendary on them, and Run Over draws the route line up to the stop where you fell.
15.q2: Before, a run just started and the only sign of progress was a 12 of 30 label. Now a thin route line sits under every header, under the battle bar, on the Continue ticket and inside the Rotom Phone, with a red diamond for every Gym.
15.q3: Yes, seven. New Run is four small steps with a step bar on top, so no step is crowded, and Run Over is kept apart from the Run Report so the sad moment and the numbers do not fight.
15.q4: The four run choices on the New Run page (kind of run, stage length, first region, seed) are the same switches as Settings › Gameplay. The phone shows the route line on its home screen.
15.q5: Yes: a quiz from Professor Oak, three starters on Poké Balls, Legendary blessings and a Hall of Fame are all classic moments.

16.name: Stage Lights
16.big: Every screen is lit like a stage. In battle the two dark bars are gone: the foe's plate floats top-left, the command console lifts off the bottom, and light beams cross a full arena. Menus now sit over the place you are (the town, or the route) instead of a flat backdrop.
16.q1: Yes. Sun rays on the title and hub, a spotlight on the picked party card, a glowing phone in the dark, light beams and a vignette in battle, a star ring for shinies.
16.q2: Pass 15 added the journey line but kept flat bars and a flat backdrop. Here the battle shows far more arena, and every menu gains depth and a sense of place. The gimmick cut-ins also get their dark stage back, so the white titles read properly again.
16.q3: Yes, four. Info and Auto were buttons with nowhere to go: Info now has its own page (weather, field, stat changes, enemy heals left), with the Battle Log one key away, and Auto has its own page for style, speed and when to stop.
16.q4: The Rotom Phone glows over a dimmed world, so the pause reads as a pause. Settings sit over the town like every other out-of-run page.
16.q5: Yes. Foe plate top-left with the arena wide open is the classic battle framing, and the shiny star ring is straight from the series.

17.name: Headlines
17.big: Big type leads every screen. The title is rebuilt around a giant logo and a word menu, battle commands are big slanted words instead of small round icons, moves are called out across the screen, the party hand fans out, and every page has its name in giant letters behind it.
17.q1: Yes. The logo is twice the size, FIGHT is the biggest thing in the battle console, and move names slam across the arena when they land.
17.q2: Pass 16 changed light and depth but kept small labels. Here the words carry the design: fewer icons to decode, faster to read at a glance.
17.q3: Yes, six. Text, Story and Save & Data were settings tiles with no page behind them; Boot, Loading and Credits did not exist at all.
17.q4: Settings now has a page behind all nine tiles. Save & Data shows backups, the save check, export and import in one place. The phone's next stop is a headline.
17.q5: Yes. Big slanted command words, loud move call-outs and a loading tip with your team walking are all series habits.

18.name: Showdown
18.big: Big fights look big. Trainer battles hang pennants in the trainer's colours and show the foe's team down the side. The next Gym is posted on the title, the phone and the party screen with who is a good pick. Gym Leaders, Legendaries and the Evil Team get their own scenes.
18.q1: Yes. Pennants, a gold-trimmed boss plate, a glowing Legendary in the dark, a spinning badge in a burst of light.
18.q2: Pass 17 made every screen louder, but a Gym fight still looked like any other. Now the stakes show: what the boss brings, how many heals are left, whether the boss power is used.
18.q3: Yes, six. Each big moment has its own page instead of sharing the normal battle or victory screens. Losing to a rival has a page that says clearly the run goes on.
18.q4: The phone carries a Next Gym poster under the run score and Rotom talks about it. Nothing new is needed in Settings; boss scenes follow the Animations page.
18.q5: Yes. Gym intro, badge ceremony, a Legendary waiting in a cave and a rival who says 'Smell ya later' are the heart of the series.

19.name: The Other Side
19.big: Evil Mode joins the redesign. The same big type, cards and word menus, but in Team Nova's black, crimson and gold, so it is clearly the same game seen from the other side. Evil Mode gets its own glowing row on the title, the Boss's shadow looms behind Red there, and the Boss gets a battle screen of his own.
19.q1: Yes. Lacquer black with crimson seams and gold numbers, a giant N behind the crew, a glass-crack split when the Hero walks in, a PAID IN FULL stamp.
19.q2: Until now the redesign only covered the hero's game. Evil Mode now has the same parts (word menu, panels, cut-ins, key strip) in its own livery, following the approved Dominion mockups for content.
19.q3: Yes, twelve. Giving an order, the odds Card, the Boss order, the result and the Hero interrupt are each their own page, so no screen has to hold a whole day. The Boss also gets his own battle page: the Hero raids the Hideout and you hold the door.
19.q4: Esc opens the Boss Menu: the title's word menu in black, with the empire at a glance beside it. Settings is the same Settings, with a Dominion category.
19.q5: Yes, the villain side of one: grunts with ranks, Persian by the Boss, Rocket as the rival gang, and Red as the trainer you do not want to meet.

20.name: Any Screen, Any Player
20.big: Built for fingers as well as keys. The title menu becomes a pad of big buttons, battle commands leave the bottom bar and sit under the right thumb with a Menu button on screen, party cards stand straight so none overlap, and every page gets a full-width button bar. Plus an answer for every screen and player: ultrawide wings, phone layouts, high-contrast, colour-blind, large-text and calm versions.
20.q1: Less about flash, more about reach: the upright phone battle with a giant FIGHT button and the patterned type wall are the eye-catchers.
20.q2: Passes 1 to 19 only ever drew one 960 by 540 screen for a keyboard. Now the Title and Battle are laid out again around a thumb, every key hint is a button you can tap, and every colour signal has a shape as well.
20.q3: Yes, seven: three for screen shapes, four for accessibility. Each is linked to the setting that switches it on.
20.q4: Battle now has an on-screen Menu button, because a phone has no Esc key. Settings › Display gains Wide screen (Wings, Scenery, Black bars). The button bar colours confirm green and back red on every page.
20.q5: Yes. The upright phone layout is the handheld layout the series grew up on: scene on top, big buttons underneath.
